# Urban Heat Islands: Why Cities Run Warmer

Urban heat islands describe the tendency of built-up areas to register
higher air and surface temperatures than the surrounding countryside,
especially after sunset. The effect arises from a combination of factors:
dark pavement and roofing absorb more solar radiation than vegetated land;
tall buildings trap heat and slow the nighttime release of warmth into the
sky; and the removal of trees and soil reduces the natural cooling that
comes from shade and evaporation.

## Contributing Factors

Several elements compound the warming:

- **Surface materials.** Asphalt and dark roofing can reach surface
  temperatures tens of degrees above ambient air temperature on a sunny
  afternoon.
- **Building geometry.** Narrow streets flanked by tall structures — often
  called urban canyons — limit how quickly heat radiates back out at night.
- **Waste heat.** Vehicles, air conditioners, and industrial equipment all
  add heat directly to the surrounding air.
- **Loss of vegetation.** Trees and grass cool their surroundings through
  evapotranspiration; paving over these surfaces removes that cooling
  pathway entirely.

## Mitigation Approaches

Researchers and municipal planners have tested a range of countermeasures,
including reflective ("cool") roofing and paving materials that bounce back
more incoming sunlight, expanded urban tree canopy, green roofs planted
with drought-tolerant vegetation, and light-colored building facades. No
single measure eliminates the effect; most cities pursue a mix tailored to
their climate, budget, and existing infrastructure.

## Why It Matters

Beyond simple discomfort, elevated urban temperatures increase electricity
demand for cooling, worsen air quality by accelerating the formation of
ground-level ozone, and raise health risks during heat waves, particularly
for older residents and those without reliable access to air conditioning.
Understanding the heat island effect at a neighborhood scale — rather than
only city-wide — helps target interventions where they will have the
greatest benefit.
